questions.q: Which type of drug is excreted from the body?
questions.exp: The chapter opens with 'Ionised / water soluble / polar drug' — only the water-soluble, polar form of a drug is available for excretion. (Book p15)

questions.q: The two major organs of excretion are:
questions.exp: The major organs of excretion are kidneys and liver; minor routes (saliva, sweat) are mentioned separately. (Book p15)

questions.q: The most common (m/c) organ for excretion is the kidney; the most common organ involved in metabolism is the:
questions.exp: The flowchart marks kidneys as the m/c organ for excretion, and the note states 'm/c organ involved in metabolism → Liver'. (Book p15)

questions.q: Besides the major organs of excretion, some drugs are excreted through:
questions.exp: 'Some drugs are excreted through saliva & sweat' — minor routes that can matter for drug detection and for side effects. (Book p15)

questions.q: According to the table of excretory mechanisms, filtration accounts for what percentage of drug excretion?
questions.exp: The table columns are headed 'Filtration (20%)' and 'Tubular secretion (80%)'. (Book p15)

questions.q: Which mechanism accounts for the majority (80%) of drug excretion?
questions.exp: Tubular secretion is labelled 80% while filtration is 20% — active tubular secretion is the dominant renal excretory mechanism. (Book p15)

questions.q: Unbound drug is excreted by:
questions.exp: Table row 'unbound drug': filtration (+) but tubular secretion (−); only the free, unbound fraction is filtered at the glomerulus. (Book p15)

questions.q: Plasma protein (negative charge) bound drug is excreted by:
questions.exp: Table row 'Plasma protein (negative charge) bound drug': filtration (−) but tubular secretion (+); tubular secretion is the route by which protein-bound drug is still excreted. (Book p15)

questions.q: Protein-bound drug is not filtered because of the:
opts: Negative charge of the basement membrane
Positive charge of the basement membrane
Large size of the drug molecule alone
Absence of porins in the glomerulus
questions.exp: The table annotates filtration (−) for protein-bound drug as 'd/t −ve charge of basement membrane' — the negatively charged glomerular barrier repels the anionic protein-drug complex. (Book p15)

questions.q: Plasma proteins carry which charge?
opts: Variable charge, depending on the drug
questions.exp: The table specifies 'Plasma protein (negative charge) bound drug' — albumin and other plasma proteins are negatively charged. (Book p15)

questions.q: A patient with hypoalbuminaemia has more unbound drug in plasma. For a drug cleared mainly by filtration, the effect is:
opts: Increased filtration and greater excretion of the drug
No change, since filtration depends only on GFR
questions.exp: It is the unbound fraction that is filtered (+); when plasma protein is low, more drug is unbound, so more is filtered and excreted — the basis for altered dosing in nephrotic syndrome. (Book p15)

questions.q: Filtration as a mechanism of drug excretion is dependent on:
opts: GFR, giving a constant rate of excretion
Plasma protein binding, giving a variable rate
Tubular reabsorption, giving a zero-order rate
Hepatic blood flow, giving a first-order rate
questions.exp: Note: 'Filtration is dependent on GFR → Constant rate of excretion' — as long as GFR is stable, the filtered amount per unit time stays constant. (Book p15)

questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a markedly reduced GFR. Which mechanism of drug excretion is most affected?
questions.exp: Filtration is dependent on GFR, so a fall in GFR directly lowers filtration-based excretion — the reason doses of renally excreted drugs must be reduced. (Book p15)

questions.q: Rate of drug elimination (RDE) is defined as the:
opts: Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body
Time taken for the drug to fall by half
Fraction of the dose reaching systemic circulation
Volume of plasma cleared of drug per hour
questions.exp: 'Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body' — RDE is expressed in mg/hr. (Book p15)

questions.q: RDE is calculated as:
questions.exp: RDE = plasma concentration × Clearance, with the units (mg/hr) = (mg/ml) × (ml/hr). (Book p15)

questions.q: The units of plasma concentration, clearance and RDE respectively are:
questions.exp: The book writes (mg/hr) under RDE, (mg/ml) under plasma concentration and (ml/hr) under clearance — these units are how the three quantities fit together. (Book p15)

questions.q: Plasma concentration is defined as the:
opts: Concentration of drug present in each ml of plasma, in mg/ml
Total amount of drug in the body in mg
Volume of plasma containing 1 mg of drug
Amount of drug bound to plasma proteins
questions.exp: 'Plasma conc: Conc of drug present in each ml of plasma → mg/ml.' (Book p15)

questions.q: Drug clearance is defined as the:
opts: Amount of plasma being cleared of the drug per hour
Amount of drug eliminated per hour from the body
Volume of distribution of the drug
questions.exp: 'Drug clearance: Amount of plasma being cleared of the drugs per hour' — clearance is a volume per unit time, not an amount of drug. (Book p15)

questions.q: The two modes of drug dosing described are:
opts: Continuous IV infusion and intermittent dosing
questions.exp: Under DRUG DOSING the two headings are (a) continuous IV infusion and (b) intermittent dosing. (Book p15)

questions.q: Infusion rate / dosing rate is also known as the:
questions.exp: 'Infusion rate / dosing rate: AKA loading dose' — a continuous infusion sets up the desired plasma level, whereas the repeated dose that sustains it is the maintenance dose. (Book p16)

questions.q: In the concentration-time curve of an IV infusion, phase I represents:
opts: Slowly rising state (infusion), where absorption > excretion
A loading dose given as a bolus
questions.exp: Phase I is the slowly rising state of infusion, during which absorption exceeds excretion so plasma concentration climbs. (Book p16)

questions.q: Phase II of the concentration-time curve represents:
opts: Peak concentration after a bolus dose
questions.exp: Phase II is the flat plateau — steady state plasma concentration, where infusion rate equals the rate of drug elimination. (Book p16)

questions.q: At the plateau of the infusion curve, the relationship between infusion and elimination is:
opts: Infusion rate = rate of drug elimination
Infusion rate > rate of drug elimination
Infusion rate < rate of drug elimination
questions.exp: The plateau is labelled 'Infusion rate = Rate of drug elimination' — the amount entering the body each hour equals the amount leaving, so the concentration stays steady. (Book p16)

questions.q: Phase III of the curve is the declining state because:
opts: The drug is redistributed to fat
questions.exp: Phase III is labelled 'Excretion > Absorption' — elimination now exceeds input, so plasma concentration falls. (Book p16)

questions.q: The infusion rate required to maintain a desired plasma concentration is calculated as:
questions.exp: 'Infusion rate = Plasma concentration × clearance' — the same relationship as RDE, since at steady state infusion must match elimination. (Book p16)

questions.q: How many half-lives are required to attain steady state plasma concentration?
questions.exp: '4–5 T1/2 are required to attain steady state plasma concentration' — this is why a loading dose is given when an immediate effect is needed. (Book p16)

questions.q: Continuous infusion dosing is stated to depend on:
questions.exp: Under the infusion curve, the bullet 'Depends on volume of distribution' applies to the infusion/loading dose, while the maintenance dose depends on clearance. (Book p16)

questions.q: According to the page, attainment of steady state depends on:
questions.exp: For continuous IV infusion the page states that steady state depends on volume of distribution. (Book p16)

questions.q: Intermittent dosing is also known as:
questions.exp: 'Intermittent dosing: AKA maintenance dose' — the dose is repeated at intervals to hold the plasma concentration steady. (Book p16)

questions.q: The purpose of the intermittent (maintenance) dose is to:
opts: Maintain plasma concentration in steady state
questions.exp: 'Dose given after a certain period of time to maintain plasma concentration in steady state' — maintenance dosing sustains, rather than establishes, the level. (Book p16)

questions.q: The maintenance dose depends on:
questions.exp: 'Depends on Clearance' — clearance governs how much drug must be replaced per unit time, whereas volume of distribution governs the loading dose. (Book p16)

questions.q: The maintenance dose is calculated by the formula:
questions.exp: Boxed formula: maintenance dose = PC × CL × Time / f, where f is bioavailability. (Book p16)

questions.q: In the maintenance dose formula, 'f' denotes:
questions.exp: [f: Bioavailability] — the fraction of the administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p16)

questions.q: For intravenous routes, the value of f is:
questions.exp: 'f = 1 in IV routes' — intravenous administration bypasses absorption barriers, so the entire dose reaches the systemic circulation. (Book p16)

questions.q: A drug with a bioavailability of 0.5 is to be given orally instead of intravenously. To maintain the same plasma concentration, the oral dose must be:
questions.exp: Since dose = PC × CL × Time / f and f falls from 1 to 0.5, the required dose doubles — oral doses are higher than IV doses for this reason. (Book p16)

questions.q: Half-life (T1/2) is defined as the time taken by a drug to:
opts: Be completely eliminated from the body
questions.exp: 'Time taken by a drug to decrease by 50% in plasma.' (Book p16)

questions.q: Half-life is directly proportional to:
opts: Volume of distribution and inversely proportional to clearance
Clearance and inversely proportional to volume of distribution
Both volume of distribution and clearance
Neither volume of distribution nor clearance
questions.exp: T1/2 ∝ volume of distribution (vd) / Clearance (Cl) — a larger distribution volume prolongs half-life; a higher clearance shortens it. (Book p16)

questions.q: The formula relating half-life to volume of distribution and clearance is:
questions.exp: T1/2 = 0.693 × vd/Cl — the constant 0.693 (ln 2) converts the first-order rate constant into half-life. (Book p16)

questions.q: Half-life equals 0.693 divided by:
questions.exp: T1/2 = 0.693 / kel — half-life and the elimination rate constant are reciprocally related. (Book p16)

questions.q: The elimination constant (kel) is equal to:
questions.exp: 'Elimination constant (kel) = Cl / vd' — the fraction of the distribution volume cleared per unit time. (Book p16)

questions.q: If the volume of distribution of a drug increases while clearance remains unchanged, the half-life will:
questions.exp: Since T1/2 = 0.693 × vd/Cl, a rise in vd with constant Cl lengthens the half-life — the drug is spread over a larger volume and cleared more slowly relative to its load. (Book p16)

questions.q: In a patient with renal failure, clearance of a renally excreted drug falls. The expected effect on the drug is:
opts: Shortened half-life with loss of effect
questions.exp: Because T1/2 ∝ vd/Cl, a fall in clearance prolongs T1/2; the drug stays in the body longer, so dose or interval must be adjusted. (Book p16)

questions.q: Zero order kinetics means elimination of a:
opts: Constant amount of drug per hour
Constant proportion of drug per hour
Increasing amount of drug per hour
Constant proportion of the dose per half-life
questions.exp: Table row 'elimination of': zero order = constant amount of drug per hour; first order = constant proportion of drug per hour. (Book p17)

questions.q: First order kinetics means elimination of a:
opts: Constant proportion of drug per hour
Constant amount of drug per hour
Saturating amount of drug per hour
questions.exp: First order: a constant proportion (fraction) of the drug present is eliminated per unit time, so the rate falls as concentration falls. (Book p17)

questions.q: In the equation RDE = (PC)^n × Cl, the value of n for zero order kinetics is:
questions.exp: For zero order kinetics the table gives n = 0, so RDE becomes independent of plasma concentration (PC^0 = 1). (Book p17)

questions.q: In the equation RDE = (PC)^n × Cl, the value of n for first order kinetics is:
questions.exp: For first order kinetics n = 1, so RDE ∝ PC — the rate of elimination is directly proportional to the plasma concentration. (Book p17)

questions.q: When the dose is constant (Cl constant), zero order kinetics gives:
questions.exp: With constant dose and clearance: zero order → RDE = constant, because a fixed amount is eliminated per hour irrespective of concentration. (Book p17)

questions.q: When the dose is constant (Cl constant), first order kinetics gives:
questions.exp: For first order kinetics RDE ∝ PC — elimination rate changes with concentration, unlike zero order where RDE stays constant. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which statement comparing zero order and first order kinetics is correct?
opts: Zero order eliminates a constant amount per hour; first order a constant proportion per hour
Zero order eliminates a constant proportion per hour; first order a constant amount per hour
Both eliminate a constant proportion per hour
Both eliminate a constant amount per hour
questions.exp: The first row of the table contrasts exactly this: zero order = constant amount per hour; first order = constant proportion per hour. (Book p17)

questions.q: If the dose is increased, the half-life in zero order kinetics:
questions.exp: In the zero order column of the 'if dose increases' row, T1/2 shows an upward arrow — with a fixed amount eliminated per hour, a bigger dose takes longer to fall by half. (Book p17)

questions.q: If the dose is increased, the half-life in first order kinetics:
questions.exp: In first order kinetics T1/2 is constant — half-life does not change with dose or concentration, which is why it is a characteristic value for the drug. (Book p17)

questions.q: If the dose is increased, clearance in zero order kinetics:
questions.exp: The zero order column of the 'if dose increases' row shows CL with a downward arrow — because the eliminating system is saturated, clearance falls as the dose rises. (Book p17)

questions.q: If the dose is increased, clearance in first order kinetics:
questions.exp: In first order kinetics CL is constant; clearance is a fixed volume of plasma cleared per hour regardless of dose. (Book p17)

questions.q: With increasing dose, the rise in plasma concentration in zero order kinetics is:
opts: Less than proportionate to the dose
questions.exp: Zero order: ↑ in PC is disproportionate (risk of toxicity) — because clearance falls with dose, a small dose increment can cause a large, dangerous rise in plasma level. (Book p17)

questions.q: With increasing dose, the rise in plasma concentration in first order kinetics is:
questions.exp: First order: ↑ in PC is proportionate — doubling the dose doubles the plasma concentration, so toxicity risk is predictable. (Book p17)

questions.q: In first order kinetics, if the dose is doubled the plasma concentration roughly:
opts: Doubles, in proportion to the dose
questions.exp: First order gives a proportionate rise in PC with dose; the disproportionate, toxicity-prone rise belongs to zero order drugs. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which variable is CONSTANT with increasing dose in first order but CHANGES (↑ T1/2, ↓ CL) in zero order kinetics?
opts: Only the rate of drug elimination
questions.exp: In the 'if dose increases' row, first order keeps T1/2 and CL constant, whereas zero order shows T1/2 rising and clearance falling with dose. (Book p17)

questions.q: Zero order kinetics is seen in drugs with:
questions.exp: Table row 'seen in drugs with': zero order — early saturation of elimination; the eliminating enzymes/transporters are overwhelmed even at ordinary doses. (Book p17)

questions.q: First order kinetics is seen in drugs with:
questions.exp: First order kinetics is seen in drugs with late saturation of elimination — the eliminating systems have ample capacity at usual doses. (Book p17)

questions.q: For a drug following zero order kinetics, the 'exception to the rule' occurs at:
opts: Lower doses, where it follows first order kinetics until saturation — hence a.k.a. pseudozero order
Higher doses, where it follows first order kinetics after saturation
Lower doses, where it becomes truly zero order
All doses equally, as no exception exists
questions.exp: Zero order column, exception row: at lower doses these drugs follow first order kinetics until saturation, and are hence also called pseudozero order. (Book p17)

questions.q: For a drug following first order kinetics, the 'exception to the rule' occurs at:
opts: Higher doses, where it follows zero order after saturation
Lower doses, where it follows zero order before saturation
Higher doses, where it becomes pseudozero order before saturation
No dose, since first order never changes
questions.exp: First order column, exception row: at higher doses it follows zero order after saturation — once the enzymes saturate, elimination becomes a fixed amount per hour. (Book p17)

questions.q: 'Pseudozero order' is the term applied to drugs that:
opts: Follow first order kinetics at lower doses until saturation
Follow zero order kinetics at all doses
Are excreted unchanged by the kidney
questions.exp: Zero order column: at lower doses they follow first order kinetics until saturation — hence aka pseudozero order; true zero order over the whole dose range is rare. (Book p17)

questions.q: Elimination kinetics of a drug whose eliminating system is saturated even at therapeutic doses is best described as:
opts: Zero order, because a constant amount is eliminated per hour
First order, because a constant proportion is eliminated per hour
Zero order only after a further rise in dose
questions.exp: Early saturation of elimination produces zero order kinetics — a constant amount per hour — with a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration as the dose increases. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which drug is specified as following TRUE zero order kinetics?
questions.exp: The zero order example list writes 'Alcohol (true zero order)' — alcohol is eliminated at a fixed amount per hour at all relevant doses. (Book p17)

questions.q: Which of the following sets are examples of zero order kinetics?
opts: Alcohol, theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin
Most drugs used in clinical practice
questions.exp: Zero order examples: alcohol (true zero order), theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin. (Book p17)

questions.q: The examples given for first order kinetics are:
questions.exp: First order column, examples row: 'most drugs' — the great majority of drugs are eliminated by first order kinetics. (Book p17)

questions.q: A patient on phenytoin has the dose increased and develops nystagmus and ataxia. The likely explanation is:
opts: Zero order kinetics giving a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration
First order kinetics with a proportionate rise in concentration
questions.exp: Phenytoin is listed among zero order drugs; here an increase in dose raises PC disproportionately (risk of toxicity) — the classic reason phenytoin needs careful, small dose increments. (Book p17)

questions.q: In a patient with a very high blood alcohol level, the rate of fall of alcohol concentration is:
opts: Constant per hour, regardless of concentration
Zero until the liver is saturated
questions.exp: Alcohol follows true zero order kinetics — a constant amount is eliminated per hour, so concentration falls linearly rather than exponentially. (Book p17)

questions.q: The zero order examples theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin are grouped because their elimination shows:
questions.exp: The table lists these drugs under zero order kinetics, which is seen in drugs with early saturation of elimination. (Book p17)

units.title: Excretion: The Drug That Leaves the Body
units.guide: Only the ionised, water-soluble, polar drug is excreted. The major organs are the kidneys — the most common organ of excretion — and the liver, which is the most common organ of metabolism, while saliva and sweat handle small amounts.

units.title: Filtration (20%) vs Tubular Secretion (80%)
units.guide: Tubular secretion (80%) dominates over filtration (20%). Only unbound drug is filtered; protein-bound drug, because of the negative charge of the basement membrane, is not filtered but is still secreted. Filtration depends on GFR and therefore gives a constant rate of excretion, so kidney disease directly reduces it.

units.title: Rate of Drug Elimination and Clearance
units.guide: Rate of drug elimination is the amount of drug eliminated per hour (mg/hr) and equals plasma concentration (mg/ml) × clearance (ml/hr). Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per hour, not an amount of drug.

units.title: Two Ways to Dose: Infusion and Intermittent
units.guide: Drugs are dosed either by continuous IV infusion or intermittently. The infusion (dosing) rate is also called the loading dose, while the repeated intermittent dose is the maintenance dose.

units.title: The Concentration-Time Curve of an Infusion
units.guide: The curve has three phases: I the slowly rising state where absorption exceeds excretion, II the steady state plateau where infusion rate equals the rate of drug elimination, and III the declining state where excretion exceeds absorption. Infusion rate = plasma concentration × clearance, 4–5 half-lives are needed to reach steady state, and the dose depends on volume of distribution.

units.title: Maintenance Dose and the Bioavailability Factor
units.guide: The intermittent dose, a.k.a. maintenance dose, is given at intervals to hold plasma concentration in steady state and depends on clearance. Maintenance dose = PC × CL × Time / f, where f is bioavailability (f = 1 for IV routes), so oral doses must be larger when bioavailability is incomplete.

units.title: Half-Life, Volume of Distribution and Clearance
units.guide: Half-life is the time taken for the plasma level to fall by 50% and is proportional to volume of distribution ÷ clearance: T1/2 = 0.693 × vd/Cl = 0.693/kel, while kel = Cl/vd. Rising vd or falling clearance (as in renal failure) prolongs the half-life.

units.title: Zero Order vs First Order Kinetics (Table)
units.guide: Zero order eliminates a constant amount of drug per hour (n = 0, RDE = constant); first order eliminates a constant proportion per hour (n = 1, RDE ∝ PC) as expressed in RDE = (PC)^n × Cl. Most drugs follow first order.

units.title: What Happens When the Dose Is Increased
units.guide: With increasing dose, zero order shows rising T1/2, falling clearance and a disproportionate rise in plasma concentration with risk of toxicity; first order keeps T1/2 and clearance constant and the plasma concentration rises proportionately.

units.title: Saturation of Elimination and Pseudozero Order
units.guide: Zero order kinetics reflects early saturation of elimination, first order reflects late saturation. The exceptions are the key exam points: zero order drugs follow first order at lower doses until saturation and are hence called pseudozero order, while first order drugs switch to zero order at higher doses after saturation.

units.title: The Example List: Alcohol, Phenytoin and the Rest
units.guide: Zero order drugs are alcohol (true zero order), theophylline, tolbutamide, phenytoin, heparin, methanol and warfarin; first order kinetics applies to most drugs. This is why a small phenytoin increment can cause toxicity and why alcohol levels fall linearly at a fixed amount per hour.
